newsitem.title: FRANCE: Protestors invade French bank board meeting.
newsitem.headline: Protestors invade French bank board meeting.

text.p: Union protestors from troubled French property bank Credit Foncier invaded a board meeting on Tuesday and threatened to hold its members until France's finance minister halted a plan to wind down the bank.
"No one is leaving this room until we hear from (French Finance Minister Jean) Arthuis," Richard Maupied, a union representative in the board room, said by mobile telephone.
Maupied said that among the Credit Foncier board members in the board room was Jean Lemierre, head of the French treasury.
The presence of Lemierre, who is the government's representative on the bank's board, could not be confirmed.
Credit Foncier board member Max Laxan confirmed to Reuters via mobile telephone that he had been forbidden to leave the room for the previous hour and a half.
"It's been quite a while," he said. "Worker representatives have come and made us aware of their worries about the closing of Credit Foncier," Laxan said.
Laxan, using a union member's mobile phone, denied that the unions had tried to contact the finance ministry.
No one at the finance ministry or treasury could be reached to comment on whether they had been contacted by the protestors.
Maupied said he was a member of the inter-union umbrella group responsible for workers' relations with Credit Foncier.

The French government announced in July it planned to wind down Credit Foncier because there was no way to save it after it announced 10.8 billion francs ($2.04 billion) of losses in 1995 and 13.6 billion francs of provisions for risky property loans and investments.
The plan outraged unions who accused Credit Foncier of overloading the books with losses to make the wind-down unavoidable.
Arthuis said on November 14 he was confident that what he calls a "managed wind-down" would go according to plan.

On November 29, French financial daily Les Echos reported that Credit Foncier would post a net attributable profit of about 660 million francs for the nine months to September 30. ($1=5.298 French Franc)
